item.title: NASA targets Feb. 19 for second Artemis II fueling rehearsal
item.description: NASA announced Monday that it is targeting February 19 for a second wet dress rehearsal of its Artemis II moon rocket after hydrogen fuel leaks and ground equipment issues disrupted testing earlier this month. The setbacks have pushed the earliest possible launch date to March 6, while ongoing concerns about the Orion capsule's heat shield continue to draw scrutiny from some space safety experts.

item.title: Google DeepMind says AlphaFold now used by 3 million researchers
item.description:
Google DeepMind leaders revealed this weekend that the company's AI-powered protein structure database has reached more than 3 million researchers across 190 countries, a milestone that underscores how artificial intelligence is reshaping scientific discovery worldwide.

In a commentary published in Fortune ahead of the India AI Impact Summit, DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis and Google Senior Vice President James Manyika outlined how the freely available AlphaFold Protein Database has become a standard tool for scientists tackling pressing global challenges. More than one-third of those researchers are based in low- and middle-income countries, according to the executives.

item.title: BHP signs $4.3B silver streaming deal with Wheaton Precious Metals
item.description:
BHP Group has entered into a $4.3 billion silver streaming agreement with Wheaton Precious Metals, marking what the mining giant describes as the largest streaming deal to date by upfront value.

Under the agreement announced Tuesday alongside BHP's half-year results, the Australian miner will deliver silver from its 33.75% stake in Peru's Antamina mine to Wheaton in exchange for an upfront payment of $4.3 billion at completion. Upon closing, expected on or about April 1, 2026, Wheaton will receive a combined 67.5% of all silver produced from Antamina, doubling its current exposure from the 33.75% it already receives under an existing stream with Glencore.

item.title: Trash piles up in Havana as US oil sanctions cripple Cuba
item.description:
Garbage is piling up on street corners across Havana, attracting swarms of flies and emitting the stench of rotting food, as Washington's campaign to cut off oil supplies to Cuba cripples the capital's waste collection system.

Only 44 of Havana's 106 garbage trucks remain operational due to fuel shortages, state media outlet Cubadebate reported this month, according to Reuters. Cardboard boxes, plastic bottles, used bags, and rags now tower at intersections throughout the coastal city, forcing motorists, pedestrians, and cyclists to navigate around the refuse.

"It's all over the city," resident Jose Ramon Cruz told Reuters. "It's been more than 10 days since a garbage truck came."

item.title: NASA says 15,000 city-killer asteroids remain undetected
item.description:
NASA's head of planetary defense has acknowledged that approximately 15,000 medium-sized asteroids capable of devastating an entire city remain undetected and untracked, leaving Earth vulnerable to a potentially catastrophic strike with little warning.

Dr. Kelly Fast, the agency's Acting Planetary Defense Officer, made the admission at the American Association for the Advancement of Science annual meeting in Phoenix, Arizona, which concluded on February 14. She said NASA has only identified about 40 percent of the estimated 25,000 near-Earth asteroids that are at least 140 meters in diameter, the threshold scientists consider capable of causing major regional devastation.

"It's truly the asteroids we are unaware of that keep me up at night," Fast said. "We aren't particularly concerned about the larger ones featured in movies since we know their locations. The smaller objects are constantly entering our atmosphere, and I'm not excessively worried about them. It's the intermediate-sized asteroids that could cause regional damage—while not necessarily global consequences—that truly concern us. And we have no idea where all of them are."

item.title: Trump to participate 'indirectly' in Iran nuclear talks in Geneva
item.description:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi arrived in Geneva on Monday ahead of a second round of indirect nuclear negotiations with the United States, meeting with the head of the U.N. nuclear watchdog as both sides signaled cautious willingness to engage while holding firm to core positions.

The talks, scheduled for Tuesday and mediated by Oman, come amid heightened military posturing in the Persian Gulf and volatile commodity markets. President Donald Trump said he would participate "indirectly" in the negotiations, calling them "very important" while asserting that Tehran is eager to reach a deal following U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities last June.

item.title: Report finds 74% of Big Tech's AI climate claims lack evidence
item.description:
A new analysis has found that the vast majority of claims from technology companies about artificial intelligence's potential to combat climate change are unsupported by evidence, with researchers warning that the energy-intensive nature of generative AI may actually worsen global emissions.

The report, released on February 17 by climate nonprofits Beyond Fossil Fuels and Climate Action Against Disinformation, examined 154 statements from industry and institutional sources claiming AI would deliver net climate benefits. According to the study, 74 percent of these assertions lacked any verifiable evidence.

item.title: Oil holds steady as US-Iran nuclear talks resume in Geneva
item.description:
Oil prices held steady on Tuesday as traders weighed supply disruption risks following Iranian naval exercises near the Strait of Hormuz, with attention focused on high-stakes nuclear talks between the United States and Iran set to begin later in the day in Geneva.

Brent crude futures edged lower by 0.2 percent, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate held near Monday's closing levels, according to Reuters. Market participants are watching whether the negotiations could ease tensions or set the stage for further escalation in a region that accounts for roughly a fifth of global oil shipments.

item.title: China's clean energy capacity surpasses fossil fuels for first time
item.description:
China has crossed a historic threshold in its energy transition, with clean energy sources now accounting for more installed power capacity than fossil fuels for the first time, according to new data from Global Energy Monitor. As of February 2026, 52% of China's operating power capacity comes from non-fossil fuel sources, while 48% is derived from coal, natural gas, and other fossil fuels.

The milestone places the world's largest carbon emitter alongside Brazil, France, and Germany as economies predominantly powered by clean energy. Yet China's continued construction of coal-fired power plants at record levels underscores the tensions between its climate ambitions and energy security concerns.

item.title: Bacteria frozen 5,000 years in Romanian cave resists 10 antibiotics
item.description: A bacterial strain preserved for 5,000 years in the ice of Romania's Scarisoara Cave has been found resistant to 10 modern antibiotics, according to research published this week in Frontiers in Microbiology. The discovery offers new insights into the ancient origins of antimicrobial resistance while raising concerns about the potential spread of resistance genes as climate change melts long-frozen environments.

item.title: EU advisers warn bloc unprepared for worsening climate change
item.description:
The European Union is unprepared for worsening climate change and must urgently increase investment to protect people and infrastructure from intensifying floods, wildfires, and severe heatwaves, independent scientific advisers warned on Monday.

The European Scientific Advisory Board on Climate Change released a report titled "Strengthening resilience to climate change – Recommendations for an effective EU adaptation policy framework," calling for a more coordinated approach across member states as the bloc faces escalating climate risks that could "undermine the EU's economic and social foundations."

item.title: Kremlin rejects European findings that Russia poisoned Navalny
item.description:
Scientists and chemical weapons experts conclude that the rare neurotoxin found in Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny's body was almost certainly synthesized in a laboratory rather than harvested from South American dart frogs, according to analysis released at the Munich Security Conference last week.

The United Kingdom, France, Germany, Sweden, and the Netherlands announced on February 14 that laboratory testing had "conclusively confirmed" the presence of epibatidine in samples taken from Navalny's body. The toxin, naturally occurring only in Ecuadorian poison dart frogs, was described as "highly likely" the cause of his death in an Arctic penal colony on February 16, 2024.

item.title: Japan to ship carbon emissions to Malaysia in regional first
item.description:
Japan will ship carbon dioxide emissions to Malaysia in what would be the first cross-border carbon capture and storage project in Southeast Asia, a plan that is drawing criticism from climate advocates who argue the technology is more symbolic than effective in combating climate change.

Under the arrangement, emissions from Japan's polluting industries—including electric power, oil refining, cement, and steel—would be captured, liquefied, and transported by ship to depleted gas fields off the coast of Sarawak on the island of Borneo. If successful, experts say the project could pave the way for similar initiatives in other Southeast Asian nations such as Indonesia and Thailand.

item.title: Experts say toxin that killed Navalny was lab-made, not from frogs
item.description:
The toxin that European governments say killed Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny was almost certainly manufactured in a laboratory rather than extracted from poison dart frogs in the wild, according to experts who spoke out this week following an announcement from five European nations.

Days after the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Sweden, and the Netherlands jointly declared that Navalny was poisoned with epibatidine, a neurotoxin found naturally in South American dart frogs, specialists in amphibian biology and toxicology told news outlets that obtaining the substance from live frogs would be practically impossible.

item.title: Chinese humanoid robots perform kung fu at world's most-watched TV gala
item.description:
China's biggest technology firms used the Lunar New Year holiday to demonstrate the country's growing dominance in artificial intelligence and robotics, with humanoid robots performing martial arts on the world's most-watched television broadcast and several leading AI developers unveiling new flagship models.

Four robotics startups—Unitree Robotics, Galbot, Noetix, and MagicLab—displayed their humanoid machines during the 2026 Spring Festival Gala on Sunday, a China Central Television event comparable in cultural significance to the Super Bowl in the United States. The gala attracted an estimated 79% of live television viewers in China last year, according to Reuters.

item.title: US and Iran begin second round of nuclear talks in Geneva
item.description:
European stocks held firm on Tuesday as investors monitored the second round of nuclear negotiations between the United States and Iran in Geneva, with energy markets also showing stability despite heightened regional tensions.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 was steady in early trading, according to Reuters, as the talks between Washington and Tehran got underway. U.S. markets remained closed for the Presidents' Day holiday, limiting trading volumes across global exchanges.

item.title: Satellite imagery confirms USS Abraham Lincoln near Iran
item.description: As diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran resume in Geneva this week, the Pentagon has assembled what analysts describe as one of the largest American naval concentrations in the Middle East since the 2025 strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. President Trump has ordered the USS Gerald R. Ford, the Navy's largest and most advanced warship, to join the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group already positioned in the Arabian Sea, creating a rare dual-carrier presence aimed at pressuring Tehran into nuclear concessions.

item.title: Iran begins Strait of Hormuz military drills ahead of US talks
item.description:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched extensive naval exercises in the Strait of Hormuz on February 16, demonstrating its military capabilities just one day before a critical round of nuclear negotiations with the United States in Geneva. The drills, titled "Smart Control of Hormuz Strait," were supervised by IRGC Commander Major General Mohammad Pakpour and aimed to test operational readiness against what Tehran described as "potential security and military threats," according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

The Strait of Hormuz, located between Oman and Iran, represents one of the world's most critical energy chokepoints. Approximately 20 million barrels of oil flow through the waterway daily, accounting for roughly 20% of global petroleum consumption, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. More than 80% of that crude oil is destined for Asian markets, with China, India, Japan, and South Korea as the primary recipients.

item.title: Scientists drill deepest-ever sediment core under Antarctic ice
item.description:
An international team of researchers has drilled a 228-meter sediment core from beneath the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, setting a record for the deepest geological sample ever retrieved from under any ice sheet. The core, which could span 23 million years of climate history, will help scientists predict how much ice may melt as the planet warms.

The achievement, announced this week by the SWAIS2C (Sensitivity of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet to 2°C) project, came on the team's third attempt after two previous Antarctic seasons were thwarted by technical challenges. The core was extracted from a location at Crary Ice Rise on the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, more than 700 kilometers from the nearest Antarctic research stations.

item.title: US and Iran begin second round of nuclear talks in Geneva
item.description:
The United States and Iran began a second round of indirect nuclear negotiations in Geneva on Tuesday, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi leading Tehran's delegation following a meeting with the head of the United Nations nuclear watchdog.

The talks, mediated by Oman, come as the U.S. military bolsters its presence in the Middle East and Iran conducts live-fire exercises in the Strait of Hormuz.
